title: Referential Dangling: How Prompt Compression Quietly Breaks Multi-Hop Answers
hook: Compressors score chunks independently, so they can keep the sentence holding the answer and delete the one defining who it's about — leaving text that reads fine and answers wrong.
key_points: Hard prompt compression scores tokens, sentences, or chunks independently and keeps the top-ranked ones under a budget.
Independent selection can split a dependent evidence pair — the authors call the survivor a 'referential dangling' reference.
At compression ratio 0.30, all six compressors tested show dangling on HotpotQA bridge examples, at rates up to 60%.
Every document in LongBench-v2 Single-Document QA contained at least one dangling reference.
Reinserting the missing supporting paragraph within the same token budget improved accuracy 29–34 points on dangling examples.
A compact classifier that reranks omitted sentences by referential need recovered 4.7 points with almost no budget increase.
content_html: Long-context inference is expensive, so a common trick is hard prompt compression: score the pieces of a document for relevance and keep only the best ones that fit a token budget. This paper identifies a structural bug in that procedure — not a tuning problem, a paradigm one.
extra_html:
The failure

Because units are scored independently, a compressor can retain a sentence that states the answer while deleting the sentence that defines the entity the answer refers to. The surviving text still reads as relevant; it just no longer means anything determinate. The authors call this referential dangling, and it hits multi-hop questions hardest, where the evidence is a chain by construction.

The measurements are blunt. At a compression ratio of 0.30, Beaver — which ranks coherent chunks with Qwen3-0.6B embeddings — leaves the answer path incomplete in 34–54% of bridge examples across three multi-hop QA datasets. On a shared HotpotQA bridge set, all six hard compressors tested show dangling, at rates up to 60%, and every document in LongBench-v2 Single-Document QA contained at least one dangling reference.

Why it matters

It isn't something a better answer model papers over: on MuSiQue, GPT-5.5 is 8.8 points less accurate on compressed contexts than on contexts retaining both supporting paragraphs. Meanwhile, swapping the missing supporting paragraph back in — while removing a nonsupporting one to hold the budget fixed — recovers 29–34 points, so the information was affordable all along, just badly chosen. The authors train a small classifier to spot omitted sentences that retained text depends on and reinsert them automatically, gaining 4.7 points on HotpotQA with Qwen3-8B while the compression ratio moves only from 0.30 to 0.31. The takeaway they push: compressors should optimize relevance and referential completeness, not relevance alone.

related.title: CompactionRL: Reinforcement Learning with Context Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents
related.hook: Long-running coding agents eventually run out of context before finishing the job. CompactionRL trains them to summarize their own history mid-task, as part of the RL objective itself.

related.title: Why RAG? Grounding LLMs in Your Data
related.hook: An LLM only knows what it was trained on — until it's stale, private, or just wrong. RAG bolts on a search step so the model answers from your data and can cite it.

flashcards.prompt: What is 'referential dangling' in prompt compression?
flashcards.back_html: Retained text contains the answer, but the deleted text defined the entity needed to interpret it — the compressor kept one half of a dependent evidence pair and dropped the other.

flashcards.prompt: Why does independent scoring cause this failure?

choices.text: Each unit is judged on its own relevance, so a pair of mutually dependent passages is never evaluated as a pair
The scoring model has too small a context window to read the document
Compression ratios below 0.30 are mathematically impossible to satisfy

flashcards.explanation_html: Hard compressors rank tokens/sentences/chunks independently under a budget. Relevance is scored per unit, so nothing in the objective preserves the link between an answer and the text that defines its referent.

flashcards.prompt: Did a stronger answer model absorb the damage?

choices.text: No — on MuSiQue, GPT-5.5 was 8.8 points less accurate on compressed contexts than on ones keeping both supporting paragraphs
Yes — frontier models reconstructed the missing referent from parametric knowledge
The paper only tested small open models, so the question is open

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors report the gap persists at the frontier: the missing referent is information the model cannot recover, not a reasoning deficit it can out-think.

flashcards.prompt: What fix do the authors propose, and what does it cost?
flashcards.back_html: A compact classifier ranks omitted sentences by whether they're needed to interpret retained text and reinserts the top candidates — no support annotations needed. On HotpotQA with Qwen3-8B: +4.7 points, compression ratio moving only 0.30 → 0.31.
